title: Joint spectral characterization of SPDC photon pairs near 2 $μ$m in (Al)GaAs-on-insulator waveguides
authors: Alexandre Z. Leger, Emil Z. Ulsig, Samuel E. Fontaine, Dileep V. Reddy, Eric J. Stanton, Lynden K. Shalm, Richard P. Mirin, Martin J. Stevens, J. E. Sipe, Nicolas Volet, Deny R. Hamel
abstract: Integrated photon-pair sources are a core component of chip-based quantum computing, communication, and metrology. Although such sources have been demonstrated at conventional telecom wavelengths, the 2 $μ$m band remains comparatively less explored, despite offering advantages for free-space quantum communication, low-loss transmission in emerging fiber networks, and integration with silicon photonic platforms. In this paper, we demonstrate spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) in straight GaAs- and AlGaAs-on-insulator waveguides. This platform offers strong second-order nonlinearity and geometry-tunable dispersion, which are advantageous for efficient on-chip pair generation. Measurements of the joint spectral intensity and heralded second-order correlation function show broadband emission around 2 $μ$m with strong spectral anti-correlations. To our knowledge, this is the first direct joint-spectral characterization of an integrated SPDC source in this wavelength regime.
summary: The paper reports the first direct joint spectral characterization of SPDC photon pairs near $2 \mu	ext{m}$ using integrated GaAs/AlGaAs waveguides. By combining time-of-flight spectroscopy with advanced numerical modeling, the authors validated their source's broadband emission and determined optimal device lengths for high-efficiency quantum light generation.
main_problem: The primary goal is the joint spectral characterization of spontaneously parametrically down-converted (SPDC) photon pairs near $2 \mu	ext{m}$ using integrated waveguides.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated broadband emission with strong spectral anti-correlations and developed a numerical model that accurately reproduces the measured Joint Spectral Intensity (JSI).
method: The study combines experimental measurements of JSI via time-of-flight spectroscopy with theoretical modeling using the biphoton wavefunction approach.
model_or_system: The physical system is an integrated photon source utilizing straight GaAs- and AlGaAs-on-insulator waveguides, which provide strong second-order nonlinearity ($\chi^{(2)}$) for on-chip pair generation.
key_observables: Joint Spectral Intensity (JSI), heralded second-order correlation function ($g^{(2)}_H(	au)$), and the SPDC conversion probability ($P_{	ext{SPDC}}$).
important_parameters: The operating wavelength regime is near $2 \mu	ext{m}$, pumped from $980 	ext{ nm}$. Key parameters include effective areas ($\approx 0.75 \mu	ext{m}^2$) and optimal waveguide lengths (e.g., $\sim 13.8 	ext{ mm}$ for GaAs).
main_assumptions: The numerical model assumes both photons reach the output without scattering, and discrepancies in absolute efficiency are attributed to uncertainties in measuring on-chip pump power.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate waveguide cross-sections, field profiles, coincidence histograms showing spectral broadening for time-of-flight analysis, and comparisons between simulated and measured JSI structures.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the necessity of $2 \mu	ext{m}$ sources to detailing the experimental setup (JSI measurement), presenting quantitative results on pair generation rates ($P_{	ext{SPDC}}$), validating these results against a detailed numerical model, and finally determining optimal device lengths.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it pushes integrated quantum light sources into a technologically important wavelength band ($2 \mu	ext{m}$) crucial for free-space quantum communication, providing necessary characterization data for quantum network components.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Magnitude of the dominant electric-field component (a) for the fundamental TE00 signal/idler mode and (b) for the TM00 pump mode, calculated for the AlGaAs waveguide geometry using the numerical model described in Section 4. Similar mode profiles are obtained for GaAs.

Fig. 3. Coincidence histograms of photon pairs from a GaAs waveguide pumped by a continuous-wave diode laser at 975 nm, measured with and without the 500 m dispersive fiber. Peak broadening arises from the fiber chromatic dispersion used for time-of-flight spectral analysis. Without the fiber, the histogram was accumulated for 90 s, yielding a coincidence-to-accidental ratio of 90. The measurement with the fiber required a 20-minute accumulation, which reduced this ratio to 4; the extended accumulation time and lower ratio account for the elevated background.

Fig. 4. Setup used to measure the heralded second-order correlation function. A half-wave plate and polarizing beam splitter (PBS) control the pump power prior to coupling into the waveguide. Residual pump light is suppressed using anti-reflection (AR) coated silicon before the down-converted signal is directed to a three-detector correlation measurement.

Fig. 5. Heralded second-order correlation function measured at different pump powers. At the lowest pump power (215 µW), we measure 𝑔(2) H (0) ≈0.06. The increase in 𝑔(2) H (0) with pump power is consistent with enhanced multi-pair generation at higher SPDC brightness.

Fig. 7. Joint-spectral intensities obtained from the time-of-flight experiment described in Section 3.2 for (a) GaAs and (b) AlGaAs. Simulated joint-spectral intensities, JSI(𝜆𝑠, 𝜆𝑖) ∝|𝜑II(𝜆𝑠, 𝜆𝑖)|2, are shown for (c) GaAs and (d) AlGaAs.
